claim: PrPC, the cellular isoform of the prion protein, serves to transduce the neurotoxic effects of PrPSc, the infectious isoform.
source: PrPC, the cellular isoform of the prion protein, serves to transduce the neurotoxic effects of PrPSc, the infectious isoform, but how this occurs is mysterious.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Biasini et al., 2012; Brandner et al., 1996; Chesebro et al., 2005; Mallucci et al., 2003) as referenced in the Introduction.

claim: The flexible, N-terminal domain of PrPC functions as a powerful toxicity-transducing effector.
source: Here, using a combination of electrophysiological, cellular, and biophysical techniques, we show that the flexible, N-terminal domain of PrPC functions as a powerful toxicity-transducing effector whose activity is tightly regulated in cis by the globular C-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from electrophysiological, cellular, and biophysical experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The activity of the N-terminal domain is tightly regulated in cis by the globular C-terminal domain.
source: Here, using a combination of electrophysiological, cellular, and biophysical techniques, we show that the flexible, N-terminal domain of PrPC functions as a powerful toxicity-transducing effector whose activity is tightly regulated in cis by the globular C-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including NMR experiments and functional assays described in the manuscript.

claim: Ligands binding to the N-terminal domain abolish the spontaneous ionic currents associated with neurotoxic mutants of PrP.
source: Ligands binding to the N-terminal domain abolish the spontaneous ionic currents associated with neurotoxic mutants of PrP, and the isolated N-terminal domain induces currents when expressed in the absence of the C-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that ligands such as PPS, antibodies, and Cu2+ ions block currents induced by ΔCR PrP.

claim: The isolated N-terminal domain induces currents when expressed in the absence of the C-terminal domain.
source: Ligands binding to the N-terminal domain abolish the spontaneous ionic currents associated with neurotoxic mutants of PrP, and the isolated N-terminal domain induces currents when expressed in the absence of the C-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI constructs that induce currents.

claim: Anti-PrP antibodies targeting epitopes in the C-terminal domain induce currents.
source: Anti-PrP antibodies targeting epitopes in the C-terminal domain induce currents, and cause degeneration of dendrites on murine hippocampal neurons, effects that entirely dependent on the effector function of the N-terminus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that antibodies POM1, D18, and ICSM-18 induce currents in cells expressing wild-type PrPC.

claim: Anti-PrP antibodies targeting epitopes in the C-terminal domain cause degeneration of dendrites on murine hippocampal neurons.
source: Anti-PrP antibodies targeting epitopes in the C-terminal domain induce currents, and cause degeneration of dendrites on murine hippocampal neurons, effects that entirely dependent on the effector function of the N-terminus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing dendritic beading in hippocampal neurons treated with D18 or POM1.

claim: The effects of anti-PrP antibodies are entirely dependent on the effector function of the N-terminus.
source: Anti-PrP antibodies targeting epitopes in the C-terminal domain induce currents, and cause degeneration of dendrites on murine hippocampal neurons, effects that entirely dependent on the effector function of the N-terminus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that deletion of residues 23-31 abolishes antibody-induced currents and dendritic toxicity.

claim: NMR experiments demonstrate intramolecular docking between N- and C-terminal domains of PrPC.
source: NMR experiments demonstrate intramolecular docking between N- and C-terminal domains of PrPC, revealing a novel auto-inhibitory mechanism that regulates the functional activity of PrPC.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data showing Cu2+-induced interaction between the N- and C-terminal domains.

claim: Intramolecular docking between N- and C-terminal domains reveals a novel auto-inhibitory mechanism that regulates the functional activity of PrPC.
source: NMR experiments demonstrate intramolecular docking between N- and C-terminal domains of PrPC, revealing a novel auto-inhibitory mechanism that regulates the functional activity of PrPC.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data and functional assays showing that disruption of N-C interaction leads to toxic activity.

claim: Prion diseases are caused by refolding of the cellular prion protein (PrPC) into an infectious isoform (PrPSc) that catalytically templates its abnormal conformation onto additional molecules of PrPC.
source: These diseases are caused by refolding of the cellular prion protein (PrPC) into an infectious isoform (PrPSc) that catalytically templates its abnormal conformation onto additional molecules of PrPC (Prusiner, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Prusiner, 1998.

claim: A prion-like process may play a role in other neurodegenerative disorders, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases and tauopathies.
source: A similar, prion-like process may play a role in other neurodegenerative disorders, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases and tauopathies, which are due to protein misfolding and aggregation (Jucker and Walker, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jucker and Walker, 2013.

claim: PrPC acts as a signal transducer that mediates the neurotoxic effects of PrPSc.
source: There is evidence that PrPC, in addition to serving as a precursor to PrPSc, acts as a signal transducer that mediates the neurotoxic effects of PrPSc (Biasini et al., 2012; Brandner et al., 1996; Chesebro et al., 2005; Mallucci et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Biasini et al., 2012; Brandner et al., 1996; Chesebro et al., 2005; Mallucci et al., 2003).

claim: The PrPC molecule consists of a partially unstructured N-terminal domain (residues 23–125), and a globular, C-terminal domain (residues 126–230) comprising three α-helices and two short, β-strands.
source: The PrPC molecule consists of a partially unstructured N-terminal domain (residues 23–125), and a globular, C-terminal domain (residues 126–230) comprising three α-helices and two short, β-strands (Zahn et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zahn et al., 2000, which describes the structure of PrPC.

claim: Deletions spanning a 21-amino acid region (amino acids 105–125) at the end of the flexible, N-terminal domain induce a spontaneous neurodegenerative phenotype with certain similarities to natural prion diseases, but without accumulation of PrPSc.
source: Deletions spanning a 21-amino acid region (amino acids 105–125) at the end of the flexible, N-terminal domain induce a spontaneous neurodegenerative phenotype with certain similarities to natural prion diseases, but without accumulation of PrPSc (Baumann et al., 2007; Li et al., 2007; Shmerling et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies by Baumann et al., 2007; Li et al., 2007; Shmerling et al., 1998.

claim: These phenotypes are dose-dependently suppressed by co-expression of wild-type PrP.
source: Importantly, these phenotypes are dose-dependently suppressed by co-expression of wild-type PrP, suggesting that the wild-type and deleted molecules interact with each other, or compete for binding to a common molecular target that mediates both physiological and pathological effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies and experimental data showing suppression of currents by wild-type PrP.

claim: The shortest deletion, Δ105–125 (designated ΔCR, for central region), produces the most severe neurodegenerative phenotype.
source: The shortest deletion, Δ105–125 (designated ΔCR, for central region), produces the most severe neurodegenerative phenotype, and requires the largest amount of wild-type PrP for rescue (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2007.

claim: Deleted forms of PrP induce large, spontaneous ionic currents, recordable by patch clamping techniques, when expressed in a variety of cell lines and in primary neurons.
source: In our efforts to understand why these deleted forms of PrP are so neurotoxic, we have discovered that they induce large, spontaneous ionic currents, recordable by patch clamping techniques, when expressed in a variety of cell lines (Solomon et al., 2010, 2011) and in primary neurons (Biasini et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Solomon et al., 2010, 2011 and Biasini et al., 2013.

claim: These currents are silenced by co-expression of wild-type PrP in the same cells.
source: Remarkably, these currents are silenced by co-expression of wild-type PrP in the same cells, paralleling the rescuing effects of wild-type PrP in transgenic mice expressing deleted PrP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing suppression of currents by wild-type PrP.

claim: The spontaneous ionic currents, or some closely associated phenomenon, play a role in the neurodegenerative phenotype of mice expressing deleted PrP.
source: This observation suggests that the spontaneous ionic currents themselves, or some closely associated phenomenon, play a role in the neurodegenerative phenotype of these mice.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation between currents and neurotoxicity.

claim: Deletion of residues 23–31 abolishes the spontaneous inward currents induced by ΔCR PrP.
source: As demonstrated in these earlier studies, deletion of residues 23–31 abolishes the spontaneous inward currents induced by ΔCR PrP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), as does addition of pentosan polysulfate (PPS), a negatively-charged glycosaminoglycan which binds to several regions within the N-terminal domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Addition of pentosan polysulfate (PPS) abolishes the spontaneous inward currents induced by ΔCR PrP.
source: As demonstrated in these earlier studies, deletion of residues 23–31 abolishes the spontaneous inward currents induced by ΔCR PrP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), as does addition of pentosan polysulfate (PPS), a negatively-charged glycosaminoglycan which binds to several regions within the N-terminal domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Antibody 100B3 (targeting residues 24–28) dramatically reduced ΔCR PrP-induced currents.
source: We tested two different anti-prion antibodies: 100B3 (Thuring et al., 2005), targeting residues 24–28, and POM11 (Polymenidou et al., 2008), which binds to the octapeptide repeats (residues 51–90). These antibodies (at concentrations of 57 nM and 33 nM, respectively), dramatically reduced ΔCR PrP-induced currents (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Antibody POM11 (which binds to the octapeptide repeats, residues 51–90) dramatically reduced ΔCR PrP-induced currents.
source: We tested two different anti-prion antibodies: 100B3 (Thuring et al., 2005), targeting residues 24–28, and POM11 (Polymenidou et al., 2008), which binds to the octapeptide repeats (residues 51–90). These antibodies (at concentrations of 57 nM and 33 nM, respectively), dramatically reduced ΔCR PrP-induced currents (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: POM11 had relatively little effect on the currents induced by ΔCR/Δ51–90 PrP.
source: As predicted, POM11 had relatively little effect on the currents induced by ΔCR/Δ51–90 PrP (Figure 1B), while 100B3 and PPS were still inhibitory (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Treatment with Cu2+-pentaglycine (100 μM) blocked spontaneous currents in N2a cells expressing ΔCR PrP, but not in cells expressing ΔCR/Δ51–90.
source: We found that treatment with Cu2+-pentaglycine (100 μM) blocked spontaneous currents in N2a cells expressing ΔCR PrP, but not in cells expressing ΔCR/Δ51–90 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cu2+ coordination to the octapeptide repeats blocks ΔCR PrP currents.
source: This result indicates that Cu2+ coordination to the octapeptide repeats blocks ΔCR PrP currents.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that Cu2+ blocks currents in ΔCR but not ΔCR/Δ51–90.

claim: The inhibitory effects of PPS, POM11, 100B3 and Cu2+ did not result from acute changes in localization or trafficking of the mutant protein.
source: Thus, the inhibitory effects of PPS, POM11, 100B3 and Cu2+ did not result from acute changes in localization or trafficking of the mutant protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no change in surface PrP levels after short-term treatment with ligands.

claim: N2a cells expressing ΔCR/E3D (in which three lysine residues at positions 23, 24, and 27 were mutated to glutamic acid and the single arginine residue at position 25 was mutated to aspartic acid) did not show any currents.
source: We found that N2a cells expressing this mutant did not show any currents (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The positive charges within the 23–31 segment are essential for ΔCR-induced spontaneous currents.
source: This result indicates that the positive charges within the 23–31 segment are essential for ΔCR-induced spontaneous currents.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that charge reversal abolishes currents.

claim: Cells expressing PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI constructs displayed spontaneous ionic currents.
source: We found that cells expressing PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI constructs displayed spontaneous ionic currents.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings.

claim: The most active currents were observed with a construct encompassing PrP residues 1–109.
source: The most active currents were observed with a construct encompassing PrP residues 1–109, with successively lower current activities seen as the constructs became shorter (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The PrP 32–109 construct was much less active, demonstrating the dependence of current activity on the 23–31 region.
source: Importantly, the PrP 32–109 construct was much less active, demonstrating the dependence of current activity on the 23–31 region (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Expression of the C-terminal domain of PrPC (Δ23–89 PrP) did not induce any currents.
source: Expression of the C-terminal domain of PrPC (Δ23–89 PrP) did not induce any currents (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI currents were sporadic in nature, and were silenced by N-terminal ligands, including PPS, 100B3, POM11, and Cu2+-pentaglycine.
source: First, PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI currents were sporadic in nature, and were silenced by N-terminal ligands, including PPS, 100B3, POM11, and Cu2+-pentaglycine (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI currents were silenced in a dose-dependent fashion by co-expression of WT PrP.
source: Second, PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI currents, like ΔCR PrP currents, were silenced in a dose-dependent fashion by co-expression of WT PrP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Removal of 23–31 region abolished the ability of WT PrPC to suppress both ΔCR and PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI currents.
source: Moreover, removal of 23–31 region abolished the ability of WT PrPC to suppress both ΔCR and PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI currents (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F), which is consistent with the observation that expression of Δ23–31 PrP does not rescue the neurodegenerative phenotype of mice expressing Δ32–134 PrP (Turnbaugh et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F, and a citation to Turnbaugh et al., 2011.

claim: The currents induced by both ΔCR and PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI were voltage-dependent, only being observed at holding potentials below −30 mV.
source: Finally, the currents induced by both ΔCR and PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI were voltage-dependent, only being observed at holding potentials below −30 mV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: Cu2+ ions, when bound to the N-terminal, octapeptide repeats, promote contact between these repeats and a C-terminal surface site encompassing helices 2 and 3.
source: Recently, Evans et al. (2016) used 1H-15N HSQC NMR to demonstrate that Cu2+ ions, when bound to the N-terminal, octapeptide repeats, promote contact between these repeats and a C-terminal surface site encompassing helices 2 and 3.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Evans et al., 2016.

claim: Deletion of residues in the central region disrupts a Cu2+-driven regulatory interaction between the N- and C-terminal domains.
source: These data suggest that deletion of residues in the central region disrupts a Cu2+-driven regulatory interaction between the N- and C-terminal domains.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from NMR data showing reduced interaction in ΔCR PrP.

claim: Two antibodies targeting overlapping epitopes encompassing helix 1 in the C-terminal half of PrPC, POM1 and D18, induced spontaneous currents in N2a cells expressing WT PrPC.
source: We found that two antibodies targeting overlapping epitopes encompassing helix 1 in the C-terminal half of PrPC, POM1 (Polymenidou et al., 2008; Sonati et al., 2013) and D18 (Doolan and Colby, 2015; Williamson et al., 1998), induced spontaneous currents in N2a cells expressing WT PrPC (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ICSM-18 induced spontaneous currents in N2a cells overexpressing WT PrPC.
source: A third anti-prion antibody with a similar epitope, ICSM-18 (Antonyuk et al., 2009), had a comparable effect, which was blocked by PPS and was absent with non-specific mouse IgG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ICSM-18 scFv-induced spontaneous currents on N2a cells overexpressing WT PrPC.
source: Like the holo-antibody, ICSM-18 scFv-induced spontaneous currents on on N2a cells overexpressing WT PrPC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), although higher concentrations were required (200 nM for the scFv version, compared to 33.3 nM for the holo-antibody), presumably reflecting the lower avidity of the monovalent scFv antibodies (Mammen, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The properties of the D18-, POM1-, and ICSM-18-induced currents were identical to those of the spontaneous currents associated with ΔCR PrP, in terms of their sporadic nature, and suppression by PPS.
source: The properties of the D18-, POM1-, and ICSM-18-induced currents were identical to those of the spontaneous currents associated with ΔCR PrP, in terms of their sporadic nature, and suppression by PPS (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment of WT PrP-expressing N2a cells with POM11 blocked POM1- or D18-induced currents.
source: In addition, treatment of WT PrP-expressing N2a cells with POM11 blocked POM1- or D18-induced currents (Figure 4B and C), similar to the inhibitory effect of POM11 on ΔCR PrP currents (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Cells expressing PrP with a deletion of residues 23–31 were resistant to current induction by POM1 and D18 antibodies.
source: Finally, cells expressing PrP with a deletion of residues 23–31 were resistant to current induction by POM1 and D18 antibodies (Figure 4D), parallel to the situation with ΔCR PrP, and emphasizing the importance of the polybasic region in antibody-induced current generation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Neither D18 nor POM1 induced currents in PIPLC pretreated cells.
source: Neither D18 nor POM1 induced currents in PIPLC pretreated cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: D18 did not induce currents in N2a cells in which PrP gene expression had been abolished by CRISPR-Cas technology.
source: Second, we demonstrated that D18 did not induce currents in N2a cells in which PrP gene expression had been abolished by CRISPR-Cas technology (Mehrabian et al., 2014) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: D18 induced currents in untransfected N2a cells, although they were smaller than in transfected N2a cells over-expressing WT PrPC.
source: Finally, we observed that D18 induced currents in untransfected N2a cells, although they were smaller than in transfected N2a cells over-expressing WT PrPC, presumably due to the lower expression level of PrPC in the former cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Fab fragments prepared from D18-induced currents on N2a cells.
source: We found that Fab fragments prepared from D18-induced currents on N2a cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The ability of the C-terminally directed antibodies to induce currents in PrP-expressing cells is not due to cross-linking of cell-surface PrP by bivalent binding, or to Fc-mediated effector functions such as complement fixation.
source: This result, along with the effectiveness of ICSM-18 scFv antibody (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), indicates that the ability of the C-terminally directed antibodies to induce currents in PrP-expressing cells is not due to cross-linking of cell-surface PrP by bivalent binding, or to Fc-mediated effector functions such as complement fixation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing that Fab and scFv fragments induce currents.

claim: The antibody 6D11 (whose epitope encompasses residues 93–109) induced currents in WT PrP-expressing N2a cells.
source: The antibody 6D11 (Pankiewicz et al., 2006), whose epitope (residues 93–109) encompasses several positively charged residues following the octapeptide repeats, also induced currents in WT PrP-expressing N2a cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: 6D11 was less potent than POM1 and D18, since the currents were much smaller, and higher concentrations were required to produce consistent effects.
source: However, this antibody was less potent than POM1 and D18, since the currents were much smaller, and higher concentrations were required to produce consistent effects (66.7 nM for 6D11, compared to 33.3 nM for POM1 and 16.7 nM for D18) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Figure 4.

claim: 6D11 and three other antibodies targeting the region 93-110 (D13, POM3, ICSM-35) did not induce currents at a concentration of 33.3 nM.
source: 6D11 and three other antibodies targeting this region, D13 (Williamson et al., 1998) (epitope: a.a. 95–105), POM3 (Polymenidou et al., 2008) (epitope: a.a. 95–100) and ICSM-35 (Khalili-Shirazi et al., 2007) (epitope: a.a. 93–105), did not induce currents at a concentration of 33.3 nM (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: POM4 (whose epitope encompasses helix 3 and β1) and POM6 (which recognizes helices 1 and 2) did not produce detectable currents when applied to WT PrP-expressing N2a cells at a concentration of 33.3 nM.
source: We found that POM4 (whose epitope encompasses helix 3 and β1) and POM6 (which recognizes helices 1 and 2) did not produce detectable currents when applied to WT PrP-expressing N2a cells at a concentration of 33.3 nM (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Treatment with D18 (33.3 nM) induced large, spontaneous inward currents in hippocampal neurons cultured from Tga20 mice over-expressing wild-type PrP.
source: Treatment with D18 (33.3 nM) induced large, spontaneous inward in hippocampal neurons cultured from Tga20 mice over-expressing wild-type PrP, and also increased the fragility of these neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: D18 did not induce any currents in neurons from Prnp−/− mice, which lack PrP expression.
source: D18 did not induce any currents in neurons from Prnp−/− mice, which lack PrP expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings.

claim: Treatment with D18 or POM1 caused dendrites to assume a characteristic 'beaded' appearance.
source: We observed that treatment with D18 or POM1 caused dendrites to assume a characteristic 'beaded' appearance, which is typical of several kinds of toxic insults, including hypoxia and glutamate-induced excitotoxicity (Hasbani et al., 2001) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and a citation to Hasbani et al., 2001.

claim: The effect of D18 or POM1 on dendritic morphology was less in wild-type neurons and completely absent in Prnp−/− hippocampal neurons.
source: This effect was less in wild-type neurons and completely absent in Prnp−/− hippocampal neurons, indicating a dependence on the expression level of PrPC (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Treatment of neurons with non-specific mouse IgG had no effect on dendritic morphology.
source: Treatment of neurons with non-specific mouse IgG had no effect on dendritic morphology (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Antibody 6D11 induced mild dendrite degeneration in Tga20 neurons.
source: Antibody 6D11, which weakly induced currents in WT PrP-over-expressing N2a cells at 66.7 nM (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) induced mild dendrite degeneration in Tga20 neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), while ICSM-35 at 33.3 nM, which did not induce currents, did not cause dendritic degeneration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ICSM-35 at 33.3 nM did not cause dendritic degeneration.
source: Antibody 6D11, which weakly induced currents in WT PrP-over-expressing N2a cells at 66.7 nM (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) induced mild dendrite degeneration in Tga20 neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), while ICSM-35 at 33.3 nM, which did not induce currents, did not cause dendritic degeneration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: POM4 (33.3 nM) and POM6 (33.3 nM) had no effect on dendritic morphology.
source: Similarly, POM4 (33.3 nM) and POM6 (33.3 nM) had no effect on dendritic morphology (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: D18 had no effect on dendritic morphology of hippocampal neurons cultured from mice expressing Δ23–31 or Δ23–111 PrP.
source: Supporting such a correlation, D18 had no effect on dendritic morphology of hippocampal neurons cultured from mice expressing Δ23–31 or Δ23–111 PrP (Figure 6), demonstrating that the N-terminal domain is essential for both the dendrotoxic and current-inducing effects of the antibody.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Co-treatment of neurons with the N-terminal ligands PPS, 100B3, or POM11 abolished D18-induced dendritic degeneration.
source: In addition, we found that co-treatment of neurons with the N-terminal ligands PPS, 100B3, or POM11 abolished D18-induced dendritic degeneration (Figure 5B–D), analogous to the way these ligands inhibit D18-induced currents (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: Treatment of neurons cultured from Tga20 mice with ICSM-18 (6.67 nM) for 48 hr caused significant beading of dendrites.
source: We observed that treatment of neurons cultured from Tga20 mice with ICSM-18 (6.67 nM) for 48 hr caused significant beading of dendrites, similar to the effects of POM1 and D18 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: At higher concentrations (33.3 nM), ICSM-18 caused significant loss of neuronal cell bodies after 48 hr of treatment.
source: At higher concentrations (33.3 nM), ICSM-18 caused significant loss of neuronal cell bodies after 48 hr of treatment (not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: ICSM-18 scFv (200 nM) induced dendritic degeneration on neurons cultured from Tga20 mice but not Prnp−/− mice.
source: ICSM-18 scFv (200 nM) also induced dendritic degeneration on neurons cultured from Tga20 mice but not Prnp−/− mice, although the effect was milder than for the ICSM-18 holo-antibody (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The N-terminal domain of PrPC acts as an autonomous effector of ionic current activity.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the N-terminal domain of PrPC acts as an autonomous effector of ionic current activity, and that basic amino acids at the extreme N-terminus are essential for this activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that the isolated N-terminal domain induces currents.

claim: Basic amino acids at the extreme N-terminus are essential for the current activity of the N-terminal domain.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the N-terminal domain of PrPC acts as an autonomous effector of ionic current activity, and that basic amino acids at the extreme N-terminus are essential for this activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing that charge reversal abolishes currents.

claim: Polybasic residues 23–31 resemble a 'protein transduction domain', originally described in the HIV Tat protein.
source: One model is based on the fact that polybasic residues 23–31 resemble a 'protein transduction domain', originally described in the HIV Tat protein (Wadia et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wadia et al., 2008.

claim: Positively charged domains are capable of penetrating lipid bilayers and creating pores, by virtue of binding to and disrupting membrane phospholipids.
source: Such positively charged domains are capable of penetrating lipid bilayers and creating pores, by virtue of binding to and disrupting membrane phospholipids (Herce and Garcia, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Herce and Garcia, 2007.

claim: The ionic current activity associated with both ΔCR and PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI is apparent only at hyperpolarized holding potentials (<−30 mV), similar to the resting potential of neurons (−60 to −70 mV).
source: Consistent with penetration of a positively charged protein domain into or across the cell membrane, we find that the ionic current activity associated with both ΔCR and PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI is apparent only at hyperpolarized holding potentials (<−30 mV), similar to the resting potential of neurons (−60 to −70 mV).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from voltage-clamp experiments.

claim: Co-expression of wild-type PrPC suppresses the ionic currents induced by ΔCR and PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI.
source: Supporting this hypothesis is our observation that co-expression of wild-type PrPC suppresses the ionic currents induced by ΔCR and PrP(N)-EGFP-GPI, a phenomenon that could be attributable to competition between the wild-type and mutant forms for a common membrane-associated target protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent suppression of currents by wild-type PrP.

claim: Three different antibodies (POM1, D18, ICSM-18) targeting the C-terminal domain all induce ionic current activity in cells expressing WT PrPC.
source: Three different antibodies (POM1, D18, ICSM-18) targeting the C-terminal domain all induce ionic current activity in cells expressing WT PrPC.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings.

claim: The epitopes of POM1, D18, and ICSM-18 are largely overlapping and encompass the outer surface of helix 1.
source: Based on crystal structures, mutagenesis studies, and peptide arrays, the epitopes of these antibodies, while not identical, are largely overlapping and encompass the outer surface of helix 1, as well as parts of the β1-α1 loop and helix 3 in the case of POM1 (Antonyuk et al., 2009; Doolan and Colby, 2015; Sonati et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural studies (Antonyuk et al., 2009; Doolan and Colby, 2015; Sonati et al., 2013).

claim: Antibodies bound to helix 1 disrupt a critical regulatory interaction between the N- and C-terminal domains, thereby liberating the N-terminal domain to produce toxic effects.
source: Rather, our results suggest that antibodies bound to helix 1 disrupt a critical regulatory interaction between the N- and C-terminal domains, thereby liberating the N-terminal domain to produce toxic effects (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data and is illustrated in Figure 8B.

claim: The N-terminal domain docks onto the C-terminal domain, thereby regulating in cis the ability of the N-terminal domain to promote toxic effector functions under normal conditions.
source: NMR studies performed here as well as previously (Evans et al., 2016; Spevacek et al., 2013) demonstrate that the N-terminal domain docks onto the C-terminal domain, thereby regulating in cis the ability of the N-terminal domain to promote toxic effector functions under normal conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data from this study and citations to Evans et al., 2016 and Spevacek et al., 2013.

claim: The docking site encompasses the POM1 epitope.
source: Of note, the docking site encompasses the POM1 epitope (Evans et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Evans et al., 2016.

claim: Deletion of the central region (in ΔCR PrP) weakens Cu2+-induced N-C interaction.
source: We also show here that deletion of the central region (in ΔCR PrP) weakens Cu2+-induced N-C interaction, consistent with the hypothesis that the toxicity of the ΔCR mutant results from disrupted regulation of the N-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data showing reduced interaction in ΔCR PrP.

claim: Helix 1 antibodies (POM1, D18, ICSM18) cause major changes in dendritic morphology of cultured hippocampal neurons when applied for longer periods of time (48 hr).
source: In addition to acutely inducing ionic currents, helix 1 antibodies (POM1, D18, ICSM18) cause major changes in dendritic morphology of cultured hippocampal neurons, in particular the appearance of blebs or varicosities, when applied for longer periods of time (48 hr) (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from morphological analysis of neurons.

claim: Antibody-induced dendritic changes are entirely dependent on the N-terminal domain of PrPC.
source: These antibody-induced dendritic changes are, like the currents induced by the same antibodies, entirely dependent on the N-terminal domain of PrPC, and are blocked by N-terminal ligands and deletions of residues 23–31.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that deletion of residues 23-31 abolishes dendritic toxicity.

claim: Chronic activation of PrPC-mediated currents leads directly or indirectly to dendritic degeneration.
source: One possibility is that chronic activation of PrPC-mediated currents leads directly or indirectly to dendritic degeneration.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on the correlation between currents and dendritic changes.

claim: Dendritic varicosities similar to those caused by anti-PrP antibodies are a characteristic feature of glutamate excitotoxicity.
source: Consistent with this possibility, dendritic varicosities similar to those caused by anti-PrP antibodies are a characteristic feature of glutamate excitotoxicity (Hasbani et al., 2001), and glutamate excitotoxicity has been implicated in the neuronal degeneration induced by ΔCR PrP (Biasini et al., 2013; Christensen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hasbani et al., 2001; Biasini et al., 2013; Christensen et al., 2010.

claim: Antibodies D13, POM1, and ICSM-18 caused acute death (within 24–48 hr) of neurons when injected stereotaxically into the hippocampus or cerebellum.
source: It has been reported that antibodies D13 (Reimann et al., 2016; Solforosi et al., 2004), POM1 (Sonati et al., 2013), and ICSM-18 (Reimann et al., 2016), but not D18 (Solforosi et al., 2004), caused acute death (within 24–48 hr) of neurons when injected stereotaxically into the hippocampus or cerebellum.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Reimann et al., 2016; Solforosi et al., 2004; Sonati et al., 2013).

claim: Klöhn et al. (2012) found that D13 and ICSM-18 were non-toxic, as was ICSM-35.
source: Using a similar protocol, however, Klöhn et al. (2012) found that D13 and ICSM-18 were non-toxic, as was ICSM-35.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Klöhn et al., 2012.

claim: Sonati et al. (2013) observed that chronic treatment (10–21 days) of cerebellar slices with several C-terminally directed antibodies, including POM1, caused neuronal death.
source: Finally, Sonati et al. (2013) observed that chronic treatment (10–21 days) of cerebellar slices with several C-terminally directed antibodies, including POM1, caused neuronal death, and they concluded that this effect was dependent on the flexible N-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sonati et al., 2013.

claim: Anti-PrP antibodies trigger several toxic mechanisms in cerebellar slices, including generation of reactive oxygen species, calpain activation and stimulation of the PERK arm of the unfolded protein response.
source: It has been reported that anti-PrP antibodies trigger several toxic mechanisms in cerebellar slices, including generation of reactive oxygen species, calpain activation and stimulation of the PERK arm of the unfolded protein response (Sonati et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sonati et al., 2013.

claim: The results have important implications for the safety of anti-PrP antibody therapies for prion and Alzheimer's diseases.
source: Our results also have important implications for the safety of anti-PrP antibody therapies for prion and Alzheimer's diseases.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing neurotoxic effects of antibodies.

claim: The results add to concerns regarding the use of anti-PrP antibodies as therapeutic tools for treatment of prion diseases and Alzheimer's disease, given the potential side-effects of these reagents on neuronal viability at nanomolar concentrations.
source: First, they add to concerns that have been raised regarding the use of anti-PrP antibodies as therapeutic tools for treatment of prion diseases (White et al., 2003) and Alzheimer's disease (Klyubin et al., 2014), given the potential side-effects of these reagents on neuronal viability at nanomolar concentrations (Reimann et al., 2016; Solforosi et al., 2004; Sonati et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data and citations to prior studies (White et al., 2003; Klyubin et al., 2014; Reimann et al., 2016; Solforosi et al., 2004; Sonati et al., 2013).

claim: Pathologic ligands that bind to PrPC could produce neurotoxic effects by disrupting the normal regulatory cis-interaction between the N- and C-terminal domains.
source: Second, our results also suggest a mechanism by which pathologic ligands that bind to PrPC could produce neurotoxic effects by disrupting the normal regulatory cis-interaction between the N- and C-terminal domains, similar to the action of the antibodies described in this study.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The Alzheimer's Aβ peptide binds to PrPC and triggers functional and structural alterations in synaptic transmission.
source: The Alzheimer's Aβ peptide, which binds to PrPC and triggers functional and structural alterations in synaptic transmission (Laurén et al., 2009), is an example of such a ligand.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laurén et al., 2009.

claim: PrPSc binds to PrPC.
source: PrPSc, which also binds to PrPC (Solforosi et al., 2007), might act in a similar fashion, although the fact that mice expressing N-terminally truncated PrPC remain susceptible to prion diseases (Supattapone et al., 2001; Turnbaugh et al., 2012) argues against this as the primary pathogenic mechanism in these disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Solforosi et al., 2007.

claim: Mice expressing N-terminally truncated PrPC remain susceptible to prion diseases.
source: PrPSc, which also binds to PrPC (Solforosi et al., 2007), might act in a similar fashion, although the fact that mice expressing N-terminally truncated PrPC remain susceptible to prion diseases (Supattapone et al., 2001; Turnbaugh et al., 2012) argues against this as the primary pathogenic mechanism in these disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Supattapone et al., 2001 and Turnbaugh et al., 2012.

claim: Natural ligands, including proteins, small molecules or metal ions, may exist, whose binding to PrPC regulates an effector activity of the N-terminal domain.
source: If so, natural ligands, including proteins, small molecules or metal ions, may exist, whose binding to PrPC regulates an effector activity of the N-terminal domain, similar to the way that we suppose anti-PrP antibodies operate.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Copper ions are examples of natural ligands, binding of which to the octapeptide repeats promotes docking of the N- and C-terminal domains.
source: Copper ions are examples of natural ligands, binding of which to the octapeptide repeats promotes docking of the N- and C-terminal domains (Evans et al., 2016; Spevacek et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Evans et al., 2016 and Spevacek et al., 2013.

claim: Previous studies have implicated the N-terminal domain of PrPC in several physiological activities of PrPC.
source: Previous studies have implicated the N-terminal domain of PrPC in several physiological activities of PrPC (Parkin et al., 2007; Pauly and Harris, 1998; Sempou et al., 2016; Shyng et al., 1995b; Taylor et al., 2005; Watt et al., 2012), some of which may be regulated by interaction with the C-terminal domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Parkin et al., 2007; Pauly and Harris, 1998; Sempou et al., 2016; Shyng et al., 1995b; Taylor et al., 2005; Watt et al., 2012).
